Let me therefore change the supposition. I shall say that I know for certain he will not put his hand in the fire and keep it there until it is consumed. I think I can predict this with the same assurance as I can predict that, if he throws himself out of the window and meets no obstruction, he will not remain suspended in the air for a moment. Suspecting an unknown madness cannot give the slightest possibility to the first event, which runs against every known principle of human nature. A man who leaves a purse full of gold on the pavement at Charing-Cross at noon might as well expect it to fly away like a feather as expect to find it untouched an hour later. More than half of human reasoning consists of inferences of this kind. They carry greater or lesser certainty in proportion to our experience of people's usual conduct in such particular situations.

71. I have often wondered why everyone, despite unhesitatingly accepting the doctrine of necessity throughout their conduct and reasoning, has been so reluctant to admit it in words. In every age, people have instead tended to profess the opposite opinion. I think the explanation is this. If we examine the operations of bodies and the production of effects by their causes, all our faculties together can carry our knowledge of this relation no further than observing that particular objects are _constantly conjoined_, and that a _customary transition_ leads the mind from the appearance of one to belief in the other. Yet although the strictest examination of the subject yields this conclusion about human ignorance, people still strongly tend to believe that they see further into nature's powers. They imagine they perceive something like a necessary connection between cause and effect. When they then reflect on their own minds and _feel_ no such connection between motive and action, they are apt to suppose that effects resulting from material force differ from those arising from thought and intelligence. But we may become convinced that our knowledge of causation of any kind goes no further than the _constant conjunction_ of objects and the mind's resulting _inference_ from one to another. Once we also find universal agreement that these two circumstances occur in voluntary actions, we can more easily admit that the same necessity belongs to every cause. By attributing necessity to the will's decisions, this reasoning may contradict many philosophers' systems. Reflection will nevertheless show that their disagreement is only verbal, not a difference in their actual view. Necessity in the sense used here has never been rejected by any philosopher, and, I think, can never be rejected. Perhaps they may claim only that the mind perceives some further connection between cause and effect in the operations of matter, a connection absent from the voluntary actions of intelligent beings. Examination alone can show whether this is so. These philosophers must establish their claim by defining or describing that necessity and showing it to us in the operations of material causes.

72. People seem, indeed, to begin at the wrong end of the question of liberty and necessity when they start by examining the soul's faculties, the understanding's influence, and the will's operations. Let them first discuss a simpler question: the operations of bodies and of brute, unintelligent matter. Let them try to form any idea of causation and necessity there beyond the constant conjunction of objects and the mind's subsequent inference from one to another. If these circumstances really make up the whole necessity we conceive in matter, and everyone also acknowledges them in the mind's operations, the dispute is over—or must at least be admitted from then on to be merely verbal. But we rashly suppose that we have some further idea of necessity and causation in external objects' operations, while finding nothing further in the mind's voluntary actions. As long as we proceed on that mistaken assumption, we cannot bring the question to any definite conclusion. The only way to correct our mistake is to go back to the earlier question: examine the narrow reach of knowledge when applied to material causes, and convince ourselves that everything we know about them consists in the constant conjunction and inference already mentioned. Perhaps we shall find it hard to accept such narrow limits for human understanding. Afterwards, however, we shall have no difficulty applying this doctrine to acts of will. These evidently have a regular conjunction with motives, circumstances, and characters, and we always draw inferences from one to the other. We must therefore acknowledge in words the necessity we have already accepted in every deliberation of our lives and every step of our conduct and behaviour.[17]

[17] Another cause may explain the widespread doctrine of liberty: a false sensation, or apparent experience, of liberty or indifference that we have, or may have, in many of our actions. Strictly speaking, the necessity of an action, whether of matter or mind, is not a quality of the agent. It belongs to a thinking or intelligent being considering the action, and consists chiefly in his thoughts being determined to infer that action's existence from preceding objects. Liberty, when opposed to necessity, is simply the absence of that determination: a certain looseness or indifference we feel in passing, or not passing, from the idea of one object to that of a succeeding object. Now, in _reflecting_ on human actions, we seldom feel such looseness or indifference. We can usually infer actions with considerable certainty from motives and from the agent's dispositions. Yet in _performing_ the actions ourselves we often feel something like it. Because we readily mistake resembling objects for one another, this feeling has been used as a demonstrative, even intuitive, proof of human liberty. On most occasions we feel that our actions are subject to our will. We imagine that we feel the will itself is subject to nothing: when someone denies this and provokes us to test it, we feel the will move easily in every direction and produce an image of itself—even towards the side it did not choose. The schools call this image a _Velleity_. We persuade ourselves that this image or faint movement could at that earlier time have been developed into the act itself. For if anyone denies this, we try again and find that we can now do it. We overlook the fact that the fanciful desire to demonstrate liberty is itself the motive of our action here. And it seems certain that, however much we imagine we feel liberty within ourselves, an observer can usually infer our actions from our motives and character. Even when he cannot, he concludes in general that he could if he knew every circumstance of our situation and temper, and the most hidden sources of our constitution and disposition. According to the doctrine just explained, this is the very essence of necessity.

73. Let us continue our attempt to reconcile opinions on liberty and necessity—the most contentious question in metaphysics, itself the most contentious science. Few words are needed to prove that everyone has always agreed with the doctrine of liberty as well as that of necessity, and that here too the entire dispute has so far been merely verbal. What do we mean by liberty when we apply it to voluntary actions? Surely we cannot mean that actions have so little connection with motives, inclinations, and circumstances that one does not follow the other with some degree of uniformity, or that one provides no inference through which we can conclude that the other exists. These are plain, acknowledged facts. By liberty, then, we can mean only _a power of acting or not acting, according to the determinations of the will;_ that is, if we choose to stay at rest, we can; if we choose to move, we can do that too. Everyone grants this hypothetical liberty to anyone who is not a prisoner in chains. Here, then, there is nothing to dispute.

74. Whatever definition of liberty we offer, we should ensure two things: _first_, that it agrees with plain facts; _secondly_, that it is consistent with itself. If we meet these requirements and make our definition intelligible, I am convinced that everyone will be found to hold the same opinion about it.

Everyone grants that nothing exists without a cause of its existence. Everyone also grants that chance, strictly examined, is merely a negative word, naming no real power that exists anywhere in nature. Yet some claim that certain causes are necessary and others are not. Here definitions show their value. Let anyone _define_ a cause without including a _necessary connection_ with its effect as part of that definition. Let him also clearly show the source of the idea expressed in his definition, and I shall readily abandon the entire controversy. But if the explanation given above is accepted, this must be absolutely impossible. Without a regular conjunction between objects, we would never have formed any notion of cause and effect. That regular conjunction produces the understanding's inference, which is the only connection we can comprehend at all. Anyone who tries to define a cause without these circumstances must use either unintelligible terms or terms synonymous with the very word he is trying to define.[18] And if the definition already given is accepted, liberty opposed to necessity, rather than to constraint, amounts to chance—which everyone agrees has no existence.

[18] Thus, if we define a cause as _that which produces any thing;_ we can readily see that _producing_ means the same as _causing_. A definition of a cause as _that by which any thing exists;_ faces the same objection. What do the words _by which_ mean? If instead we had said that a cause is _that_ after which _any thing constantly exists;_ we would have understood the terms. For this is, in fact, everything we know about the matter. This constancy is the very essence of necessity, and we have no other idea of it.

chapters.title: Section 8: OF LIBERTY AND NECESSITY. — Part 2
paragraphs: 75. No method of argument is more common in philosophical disputes, or more deserving of blame, than trying to refute a hypothesis by alleging that it has dangerous consequences for religion and morality. An opinion that leads to absurdities is certainly false; an opinion with dangerous consequences is not necessarily false. Such arguments should therefore be avoided altogether. They do nothing to discover truth and serve only to make an opponent personally odious. I make this general observation without claiming any advantage from it. I willingly submit to an examination of this kind, and venture to affirm that the doctrines of necessity and liberty, as explained above, are not only consistent with morality but absolutely essential to sustaining it.

Necessity can be defined in two ways, corresponding to the two definitions of _cause_, of which it is an essential part. It consists either in the constant conjunction of similar objects or in the understanding's inference from one object to another. Now, necessity in both these senses—which are really the same at bottom—has everywhere been accepted, though silently, as belonging to the human will: in the schools, in the pulpit, and in everyday life. Nobody has ever claimed to deny that we can draw inferences about human actions, or that these inferences rest on the experienced union of similar actions with similar motives, inclinations, and circumstances. There are only two possible points of disagreement. Someone may refuse to call this property of human actions necessity. But as long as the meaning is understood, I hope the word can do no harm. Or he may maintain that we can discover something further in the operations of matter. Whatever importance that claim has for natural philosophy or metaphysics, it admittedly has none for morality or religion. We may be mistaken here in asserting that we have no idea of any other necessity or connection in the actions of bodies. But surely we attribute nothing to the mind's actions beyond what everyone does, and must readily, admit. We change no part of the accepted orthodox system concerning the will, only its account of material objects and causes. At the very least, therefore, no doctrine could be more harmless.

76. Since all laws rest on rewards and punishments, they assume as a fundamental principle that these motives influence the mind regularly and uniformly, both producing good actions and preventing evil ones. We may call this influence whatever we please. But because it is usually conjoined with the action, it must count as a _cause_, and as an instance of the necessity we are trying to establish here.

Only a person or creature capable of thought and consciousness can properly be an object of hatred or vengeance. When criminal or harmful actions arouse that passion, they do so only through their relation or connection to the person. Actions are by their nature temporary and passing. Unless they arise from some _cause_ in the character and disposition of the person who performs them, they can bring him neither honour when good nor disgrace when evil. The actions themselves may deserve blame and violate every rule of morality and religion. But the person is not accountable for them. Since they arose from nothing lasting and constant within him and leave nothing of that kind behind, they cannot make him an object of punishment or vengeance. On the principle that denies necessity, and therefore causes, a man remains as pure and untainted after committing the most horrible crime as at the first moment of his birth. His character has no involvement in his actions, because they do not arise from it; the wickedness of his actions can never establish the depravity of his character.

People are not blamed for actions they perform in ignorance and by accident, whatever the consequences. Why? Because the principles behind such actions are only momentary and end with the actions themselves. People receive less blame for hasty, unpremeditated actions than for deliberate ones. For what reason? Because a hasty temper, although a constant cause or principle in the mind, acts only at intervals and does not infect the whole character. Again, repentance wipes away every crime when accompanied by a reform of life and manners. How can we explain this? Only by saying that actions make a person criminal insofar as they demonstrate criminal principles in his mind. When those principles change and the actions cease to provide sound evidence of them, the actions likewise cease to make him criminal. But without the doctrine of necessity they never provided sound evidence in the first place, and consequently never made him criminal.

77. The same arguments make it equally easy to prove that _liberty_, in the definition given above on which everyone agrees, is also essential to morality. Without it, no human action can possess moral qualities or be an object of approval or dislike. Actions engage our moral feelings only insofar as they reveal inward character, passions, and affections. They therefore cannot give rise to praise or blame when they do not proceed from these principles but arise wholly from external force.

78. I do not claim to have anticipated or removed every objection to this account of necessity and liberty. I can foresee further objections drawn from subjects we have not discussed here. Someone might say, for instance, that if voluntary actions follow the same laws of necessity as matter's operations, an unbroken chain of necessary causes, ordained and determined in advance, extends from the original cause of everything to every single act of will of every human being. There is then no contingency anywhere in the universe, no indifference, no liberty. Even while acting, we are being acted upon. The ultimate Author of all our acts of will is the world's Creator. He first set this immense machine in motion and placed every being in the particular position from which every later event must result by inevitable necessity. Human actions, therefore, either contain no moral wickedness at all, since they arise from so good a cause, or, if they contain any wickedness, must implicate our Creator in the same guilt, since he is acknowledged as their ultimate cause and author. A man who sets off a mine is responsible for every consequence, whether the train he used is long or short. Likewise, wherever an unbroken chain of necessary causes is established, the Being, finite or infinite, who produces the first is also the author of all the rest, and must receive both the blame and the praise belonging to them. Our clear and unchangeable ideas of morality establish this rule on unquestionable grounds when we examine the consequences of a human action. Those grounds must have still greater force when applied to the acts of will and intentions of an infinitely wise and powerful Being. Ignorance or powerlessness may excuse so limited a creature as man; such imperfections have no place in our Creator. He foresaw, ordained, and intended all those human actions we so rashly call criminal. We must therefore conclude either that they are not criminal or that the Deity, rather than man, is accountable for them. But since either position is absurd and impious, the doctrine from which they follow cannot possibly be true: it faces all the same objections. A necessary but absurd consequence proves the original doctrine absurd, just as criminal actions make their original cause criminal if the connection between them is necessary and avoidable.

This objection has two parts, which we shall examine separately. _First_, if a necessary chain traces human actions back to the Deity, they cannot be criminal. The Being from whom they arise is infinitely perfect and can intend only what is entirely good and praiseworthy. Or, _Secondly_, if those actions are criminal, we must withdraw the perfection we attribute to the Deity and acknowledge him as the ultimate author of guilt and moral wickedness in all his creatures.

79. The answer to the first objection seems clear and convincing. After closely examining all natural phenomena, many philosophers conclude that the WHOLE, viewed as a single system, is ordered with perfect benevolence at every stage of its existence. In the end, they say, all created beings will enjoy the greatest possible happiness, unmixed with any positive or absolute evil or misery. Every physical evil forms an essential part of this benevolent system. Even the Deity himself, considered as a wise agent, could not remove it without allowing a greater evil or preventing a greater good that will result from it. Some philosophers, including the ancient _Stoics_, drew from this theory a source of consolation in every affliction. They taught their pupils that the evils they suffered were really benefits to the universe, and that from a broad enough viewpoint to comprehend nature's entire system, every event would become an occasion for joy and exultation. This argument, however plausible and sublime, soon proved weak and ineffective in practice. Surely you would irritate rather than soothe a man tormented by gout if you preached to him about the rightness of the general laws that produced the malignant humours in his body and carried them along their proper channels to the sinews and nerves, where they now cause such acute suffering. These expansive views may briefly please the imagination of a speculative thinker living in comfort and security. But even when pain and passion do not disturb him, they cannot remain constantly in his mind, much less hold their ground against such powerful opponents. The affections take a narrower and more natural view of their object. Through an arrangement better suited to the weakness of human minds, they concern themselves only with the beings around us and respond to events that appear good or bad within our private sphere.

80. _Moral_ evil stands in the same position as _physical_ evil. We cannot reasonably suppose that distant considerations which have so little effect on the one will exert greater influence on the other. Nature has formed the human mind so that certain characters, dispositions, and actions immediately arouse approval or blame. No emotions are more essential to its structure and constitution. The characters we approve chiefly contribute to the peace and security of human society; those we blame chiefly tend to public harm and disturbance. We may therefore reasonably suppose that moral feelings arise, directly or indirectly, from reflection on these opposing interests. What if philosophical meditation establishes a different opinion or conjecture: that everything is right in relation to the WHOLE, and that qualities disturbing society are, overall, as beneficial and as consistent with nature's primary intention as those more directly promoting its happiness and welfare? Can such remote, uncertain speculations outweigh the feelings arising from a natural and immediate view of the objects? When a man is robbed of a considerable sum, do these sublime reflections diminish his distress over the loss at all? Why, then, should we suppose that his moral resentment of the crime is incompatible with them? Or why should acknowledging a real distinction between vice and virtue not be reconcilable with every speculative system of philosophy, just as acknowledging a real distinction between personal beauty and deformity is? Both distinctions rest on the natural feelings of the human mind. No philosophical theory or speculation whatever can control or alter those feelings.

81. The _second_ objection has no equally easy and satisfactory answer. Nor can we clearly explain how the Deity can be the indirect cause of all human actions without being the author of sin and moral wickedness. Natural, unaided reason is poorly equipped to handle these mysteries. Whatever system she adopts, every step she takes in such subjects entangles her in inextricable difficulties and even contradictions. Reconciling the indifference and contingency of human actions with foreknowledge, or defending absolute decrees while clearing the Deity of authorship of sin, has so far proved beyond all philosophy's power. Happy philosophy, if this teaches her how rashly she pries into these sublime mysteries! May she leave this scene of obscurity and perplexity and return, with fitting modesty, to her true and proper field: the examination of ordinary life. There she will find difficulties enough to occupy her inquiries, without sailing into so boundless an ocean of doubt, uncertainty, and contradiction!

chapters.title: Section 9: OF THE REASON OF ANIMALS.
paragraphs: 82. All our reasoning about matters of fact rests on a kind of Analogy. It leads us to expect a cause to produce the same events we have observed arising from similar causes. When the causes are entirely alike, the analogy is perfect, and we regard the inference drawn from it as certain and conclusive. Nobody seeing a piece of iron doubts that it will have weight or that its parts will hold together, as in every previous instance he has observed. When objects are less exactly alike, however, the analogy is less perfect and the inference less conclusive, though it retains some force in proportion to the degree of resemblance. Through this kind of reasoning we extend anatomical observations made on one animal to all animals. Certainly, when blood circulation, for example, is clearly demonstrated in one creature, such as a frog or fish, this gives us strong grounds for supposing the same principle operates in all. These analogical observations can extend still further, even to the science we are now discussing. Any theory explaining how the human understanding works, or the origin and connection of human passions, gains additional authority if we find that the same theory is needed to explain the same phenomena in all other animals. We shall test this with the hypothesis used in the preceding discussion to account for all reasoning from experience. I hope this new viewpoint will confirm all our earlier observations.

83. _First_, animals evidently learn many things from experience, just as people do, and infer that the same events will always follow the same causes. In this way they learn the more obvious properties of external objects. From birth onwards, they gradually accumulate knowledge of the nature of fire, water, earth, stones, heights, depths, and so on, and of the effects these produce. Here the ignorance and inexperience of the young stand out plainly against the cunning and intelligence of the old. Long observation has taught the older animals to avoid what hurt them and pursue what brought comfort or pleasure. A horse accustomed to the field learns how high it can jump and never attempts anything beyond its strength and ability. An old greyhound leaves the more exhausting part of the chase to the younger dogs and positions himself to intercept the hare when she doubles back. The judgments he makes here rest on nothing but observation and experience.

The effects of discipline and education on animals make this still clearer. By properly applying rewards and punishments, we can teach them any course of action, even one utterly opposed to their natural instincts and inclinations. Is it not experience that makes a dog fear pain when you threaten him or raise the whip to beat him? Is it not experience, too, that makes him answer to his name? From that arbitrary sound he infers that you mean him rather than one of his companions, and that you intend to call him when you pronounce it in a particular way, with a particular tone and accent.

In all these cases, the animal evidently infers a fact beyond what immediately reaches its senses. This inference rests entirely on past experience: from the object now present, the creature expects the same consequences it has always observed following similar objects.

84. _Secondly_, the animal cannot possibly base this inference on an argument or process of reasoning through which it concludes that similar events must follow similar objects and that nature will always operate regularly. If such arguments really exist, they must surely be too abstruse for such imperfect understandings to discover. Even a philosophical genius might need the greatest care and attention to find and recognize them. Animals, therefore, are not guided by reasoning in these inferences. Neither are children, nor most people in their ordinary actions and conclusions. Nor are philosophers themselves: in the active parts of life they are, for the most part, like ordinary people and follow the same rules. Nature must have supplied another principle, one more readily and generally useful and applicable. An operation so enormously important to life as inferring effects from causes cannot be entrusted to the uncertain process of reasoning and argument. Even if this were doubtful in the case of human beings, it seems beyond question in the case of beasts. Once the conclusion is firmly established for one, every rule of analogy gives us strong grounds for accepting it universally, without exception or reservation. Custom alone prompts animals, from every object that reaches their senses, to infer its usual companion. It carries their imagination from the appearance of one to a conception of the other in that particular manner we call _belief_. No other explanation can be given of this operation in any of the higher or lower classes of sentient beings that come within our notice and observation [19].

[19] Since all reasoning about facts or causes comes merely from custom, someone may ask why people so greatly surpass animals in reasoning, and why one person so greatly surpasses another. Does the same custom not influence everyone in the same way?
Here we shall try to explain briefly the great differences between human understandings. Afterwards, it will be easy to grasp why human beings differ from animals in this respect.

1. After living for some time and growing accustomed to nature's uniformity, we acquire a general habit of extending what we know to what we do not know, imagining the unknown to resemble the known. Through this general principle of habit, we treat even a single experiment as a basis for reasoning. If the experiment was performed accurately and free from any outside circumstances, we expect a similar event with some degree of certainty. Observing the consequences of things is therefore considered very important. Since one person may far surpass another in attention, memory, and observation, this will produce a great difference in their reasoning.

2. When a complex combination of causes produces an effect, one mind may have a much wider reach than another. It may grasp the entire system of objects more readily and infer their consequences more accurately.
3. One person can follow a chain of consequences further than another person can carry the same reasoning.
4. Few people can think for long without confusing their ideas and mistaking one for another. This weakness varies in degree from person to person.

5. The circumstance on which an effect depends is often entangled with other circumstances that are external and irrelevant to it. Separating it from them often demands close attention, precision, and subtlety.

6. Drawing general rules from particular observations is a very delicate task. Mistakes in it are extremely common, whether through haste or through a narrow mind's failure to look at every side of the matter.
7. In reasoning by analogy, the better reasoner will be the person with more experience, or the one more readily able to suggest appropriate analogies.
8. Prejudice, education, passion, party allegiance, and similar sources of bias weigh more heavily on some minds than on others.
9. Once we have learned to trust human testimony, books and conversation expand one person's range of experience and thought much more than they expand another's.
Many other circumstances accounting for differences between people's understandings could easily be identified and added to these.

85. Although animals acquire much of their knowledge through observation, they also receive much directly from nature's original hand. This knowledge far exceeds the abilities they display on ordinary occasions, and even the longest practice and experience bring little or no improvement in it. We call these abilities Instincts, and are apt to marvel at them as something extraordinary that all the inquiries of human understanding cannot explain. Our wonder may diminish or cease, however, when we consider that reasoning from experience itself—the reasoning we share with beasts, on which the whole conduct of life depends—is only a kind of instinct or mechanical power. It acts within us without our understanding it, and its principal operations are not guided by the relations or comparisons of ideas that properly belong to our intellectual faculties. The instincts differ, but what teaches a person to avoid fire is still an instinct, just as much as what teaches a bird so precisely the art of incubation and the entire management and order of its nursery.

chapters.title: Section 10: OF MIRACLES. — Part 1
paragraphs: 86. In Dr. Tillotson's writings there is an argument against the _real presence_ as concise, elegant, and powerful as any argument could be against a doctrine so little deserving of serious refutation. Everyone acknowledges, says that learned prelate, that the authority of scripture and tradition rests solely on the apostles' testimony. They witnessed the miracles by which our Saviour proved his divine mission. Our evidence for the truth of the _Christian_ religion is therefore weaker than our evidence for the truth of our senses. Even for the first founders of our religion, it was no stronger; it must plainly diminish as it passes from them to their disciples. Nor can anyone place as much confidence in their testimony as in the immediate object of his own senses. But weaker evidence can never overturn stronger evidence. Consequently, even if scripture revealed the doctrine of the real presence with the utmost clarity, accepting it would directly violate the rules of sound reasoning. It contradicts the senses, although neither scripture nor tradition, on which it supposedly rests, carries evidence as strong as that of the senses—when these are treated simply as external evidence, rather than brought home to each person's heart through the Holy Spirit's immediate action.

Nothing is more useful than a decisive argument of this kind. It must at least _silence_ the most arrogant bigotry and superstition and free us from their intrusive demands. I flatter myself that I have found a similar argument. If sound, it will permanently restrain every kind of superstitious delusion among the wise and learned, and will therefore remain useful as long as the world lasts. For I presume that accounts of miracles and prodigies will continue that long in every history, sacred and secular.

87. Experience is our only guide when we reason about matters of fact. Yet we must acknowledge that this guide is not wholly infallible and sometimes leads us into error. Someone in our climate who expected better weather in any week of June than in a week of December would reason correctly and in accordance with experience. Nevertheless, events might certainly prove him mistaken. In that case, however, he would have no grounds to complain of experience: through the conflicting events that careful observation reveals, experience generally warns us of the uncertainty beforehand. Not every effect follows its supposed cause with equal certainty. Some events have always been found conjoined in every country and age. Others have proved more variable and have sometimes disappointed our expectations. Our reasoning about matters of fact thus admits every imaginable degree of assurance, from the greatest certainty down to the weakest kind of moral evidence.

A wise person therefore makes his belief proportionate to the evidence. Where a conclusion rests on unfailing experience, he expects the event with the highest assurance and treats past experience as complete _proof_ that it will occur. Elsewhere he proceeds more cautiously. He weighs the opposing experiments and considers which side has the greater number in its favour. Towards that side he inclines, with doubt and hesitation. When he finally settles his judgment, the evidence amounts to no more than what we properly call _probability_. All probability therefore assumes a conflict between experiments and observations, with one side outweighing the other and producing a degree of evidence proportionate to its advantage. A hundred instances or experiments on one side and fifty on the other leave an event's occurrence doubtful. A hundred uniform experiments against only one conflicting instance reasonably give a fairly strong assurance. Whenever experiments oppose one another, we must weigh them and subtract the smaller number from the greater to discover the exact strength of the stronger evidence.

88. To apply these principles to a particular case, consider that no reasoning is more common, more useful, or more necessary to human life than reasoning based on people's testimony and the reports of eyewitnesses and observers. Someone may deny that this reasoning rests on the relation of cause and effect. I shall not argue over a word. It is enough to observe that our confidence in any such argument comes solely from observing the truthfulness of human testimony and the usual agreement between facts and witnesses' reports. Our general rule is that no objects have a discoverable connection with one another, and that every inference from one to another rests merely on our experience of their constant, regular conjunction. Plainly, then, we should make no exception for human testimony. Its connection with an event seems in itself no more necessary than any other connection. Suppose memory did not retain things to some degree; suppose people did not generally incline towards truth and possess a principle of honesty; suppose they felt no shame when caught lying. If experience had not shown us, I say, that these qualities belong to human nature, we would never place the slightest confidence in human testimony. A delirious man, or one notorious for lying and villainy, carries no authority with us at all.

Evidence from witnesses and human testimony rests on past experience and therefore varies with that experience. We regard it as either _proof_ or _probability_, depending on whether the conjunction between a particular kind of report and a particular kind of object has proved constant or variable. Every judgment of this kind requires us to consider several circumstances. The final standard for settling any resulting dispute always comes from experience and observation. Where experience is not entirely uniform on either side, our judgments inevitably conflict. Arguments oppose and cancel one another, just as in every other kind of evidence. We often hesitate over other people's reports. We weigh the opposing circumstances that create doubt or uncertainty, and when one side proves stronger, we incline towards it. Yet our assurance still diminishes in proportion to the strength of the opposing side.

89. In this case, conflicting evidence may arise from several different sources: contradictory testimony; the witnesses' character or number; the way they give their testimony; or all these circumstances together. We suspect a reported fact when witnesses contradict one another, when there are few of them or their character is doubtful, when they have an interest in what they affirm, or when they testify hesitantly—or, at the other extreme, make excessively forceful assertions. Many other details of the same kind can weaken or destroy an argument based on human testimony.

Suppose, for example, that the fact the testimony seeks to establish has an extraordinary and marvellous character. The evidence supplied by that testimony then loses a greater or smaller amount of its strength in proportion to how unusual the fact is. We trust witnesses and historians not because we perceive _a priori_ any _connection_ between testimony and reality, but because we are accustomed to finding agreement between them. When the reported fact is something we have seldom observed, however, two opposing experiences compete. Each cancels the other as far as its strength allows, and the stronger influences the mind only through its remaining force. The very principle of experience that gives us a certain confidence in witnesses' testimony also gives us, in this case, a certain confidence against the fact they are trying to establish. These opposing grounds necessarily counterbalance one another, mutually reducing belief and authority.

_I should not believe such a story were it told me by Cato_ was a proverb in Rome even while that philosophical patriot was alive.[20] People acknowledged that a fact's incredibility could outweigh even so great an authority.
[20] Plutarch, in vita Catonis.

The Indian prince who refused to believe the first reports of frost's effects reasoned correctly. Naturally, very strong testimony was needed to make him accept facts arising from a condition of nature unfamiliar to him, with so little analogy to the events he had constantly and uniformly experienced. Although these facts did not contradict his experience, they did not conform to it either.[21]

[21] Clearly, no Indian could have experienced water failing to freeze in cold climates. This places nature in a situation entirely unknown to him, whose result he cannot predict _a priori_. It is a new experiment, and the outcome of a new experiment is always uncertain. Analogy sometimes allows us to guess what will follow, but it remains only a guess. We must admit that freezing, in this case, happens contrary to the rules of analogy and is something a rational Indian would not expect. Cold does not act on water gradually in proportion to its degree. At the freezing point, water passes in an instant from complete fluidity to perfect hardness. Such an event may therefore be called _extraordinary_ and requires fairly strong testimony to make it credible to people in a warm climate. It is still not _miraculous_, however, nor does it contradict uniform experience of nature's course in cases where all the circumstances are alike. The inhabitants of Sumatra have always seen liquid water in their own climate, and the freezing of their rivers would count as a prodigy. But they have never seen water in Muscovy during winter, so they cannot reasonably be certain what would happen there.

90. To increase the probability against the witnesses' testimony, however, suppose the fact they affirm is actually miraculous, rather than merely marvellous. Suppose also that their testimony, taken separately and by itself, amounts to complete proof. Proof then confronts proof. The stronger must prevail, but its force is still reduced in proportion to the force of its opponent.

A miracle violates the laws of nature. Since firm and unvarying experience has established these laws, the proof against a miracle, arising from the very nature of the fact, is as complete as any argument from experience could possibly be. Why is it more than merely probable that everyone must die, that lead cannot remain suspended in the air by itself, or that fire consumes wood and is extinguished by water? Because these events conform to nature's laws, and preventing them would require those laws to be violated—in other words, a miracle. We count nothing as a miracle if it ever occurs in nature's ordinary course. A man who seems healthy may die suddenly without a miracle: however unusual such a death compared with others, it has frequently been observed. But a dead man returning to life is a miracle, because this has never been observed in any age or country. Uniform experience must therefore stand against every miraculous event; otherwise the event would not deserve that name. Since uniform experience amounts to proof, the nature of the fact supplies a direct and complete _proof_ against any miracle's occurrence. Only a stronger opposing proof can overturn it or make the miracle credible.[22]

[22] Sometimes an event may not seem _in itself_ to violate nature's laws. Yet, if it really occurred, particular circumstances might make it a miracle, because it would _in fact_ violate those laws. Suppose someone claiming divine authority commanded a sick person to recover, a healthy man to fall dead, the clouds to pour rain, or the winds to blow. In short, suppose he ordered many natural events, which immediately followed his commands. These could rightly be considered miracles, since in this case they really would contradict nature's laws. If any suspicion remains that event and command coincided accidentally, there is no miracle and no violation of natural law. Remove that suspicion, and a miracle and a violation of those laws plainly remain: nothing could be more contrary to nature than a human voice or command having such influence. A precise definition of a miracle is _a transgression of a law of nature by a particular volition of the Deity, or by the interposition of some invisible agent_. People may or may not be able to detect a miracle; that does not change its nature or essence. A house or ship rising into the air is a visible miracle. A feather rising when the wind falls even slightly short of the force needed to lift it is just as real a miracle, although less perceptible to us.

91. The obvious consequence—and a general rule deserving our attention—is this: 'That no testimony is sufficient to establish a miracle, unless the testimony be of such a kind, that its falsehood would be more miraculous, than the fact, which it endeavours to establish; and even in that case there is a mutual destruction of arguments, and the superior only gives us an assurance suitable to that degree of force, which remains, after deducting the inferior.' If someone tells me he saw a dead man brought back to life, I immediately ask myself which is more probable: that this person is deceiving me or has been deceived, or that the event he describes actually occurred. I weigh one miracle against the other. I decide according to which carries the greater weight, always rejecting the greater miracle. Only if the falsehood of his testimony would be more miraculous than the event he reports can he claim to command my belief or opinion—and not before.

chapters.title: Section 10: OF MIRACLES. — Part 2
paragraphs: 92. In the preceding argument we allowed that the testimony supporting a miracle might amount to complete proof, and that its falsehood would itself be a real prodigy. But we can easily show that this concession was far too generous: no miraculous event has ever been established by evidence so complete.

For _first_, nowhere in all history can we find a miracle attested by enough people whose unquestionable good sense, education, and learning protect us against their being deluded; whose undoubted honesty puts them beyond suspicion of intending to deceive others; and whose standing and reputation give them a great deal to lose if caught lying. At the same time, the facts they attest must have occurred so publicly, and in so well-known a part of the world, that exposure would be unavoidable. Every one of these circumstances is needed to give us full assurance in human testimony.

93. _Secondly_, human nature contains a principle which, closely examined, greatly diminishes the assurance we might otherwise gain from human testimony about any prodigy. In our reasoning, we ordinarily follow this rule: objects we have not experienced resemble those we have; what we have found most usual is always most probable; and when arguments conflict, we should prefer those supported by the greatest number of past observations. Following this rule, we readily reject facts that are unusual and incredible to an ordinary degree. Yet when we go further, the mind does not always keep to the same rule. When something utterly absurd and miraculous is asserted, the mind is all the readier to accept it because of the very circumstance that should destroy its authority. The _surprise_ and _wonder_ aroused by miracles are pleasant emotions, and noticeably incline us to believe the events that produce them. This goes so far that even people unable to enjoy this pleasure directly, because they cannot believe the miraculous events reported to them, still like to share the satisfaction second-hand or by reflection. They take pride and delight in arousing other people's amazement.

How eagerly people receive travellers' miraculous accounts: descriptions of monsters on land and sea, tales of wonderful adventures, strange peoples, and unfamiliar customs! But when religious zeal joins the love of wonder, common sense disappears, and human testimony loses every claim to authority. A religious devotee may be an enthusiast who imagines seeing something unreal. He may know his story is false yet persist in it with the best intentions, hoping to advance so holy a cause. Even without this delusion, vanity under so powerful a temptation acts on him more strongly than it acts on other people in any other circumstances; self-interest has equal force. His listeners may lack—and commonly do lack—the judgment needed to examine his evidence. Whatever judgment they possess, they surrender on principle when faced with such sublime and mysterious subjects. Even if they were entirely willing to use it, passion and a heated imagination disrupt its regular operation. Their credulity increases his impudence, and his impudence overwhelms their credulity.

At its highest pitch, eloquence leaves little room for reasoning or reflection. Addressing itself wholly to imagination or the affections, it captivates willing listeners and subdues their understanding. Fortunately, it seldom reaches that pitch. Yet by stirring such coarse and common passions, every _Capuchin_, every travelling or settled teacher, can achieve with most people—and to a greater degree—what a Tully or a Demosthenes could scarcely achieve with a Roman or Athenian audience.

In every age, many invented miracles, prophecies, and supernatural events have been exposed by contrary evidence or have exposed themselves through their absurdity. These sufficiently demonstrate humanity's strong inclination towards the extraordinary and marvellous, and should reasonably make us suspicious of every such account. This is how we naturally think even about the most ordinary and credible events. Take reports of marriages. No rumours arise more easily or spread faster, especially in rural districts and provincial towns. Two young people of equal standing can hardly meet twice before the whole neighbourhood pairs them off. The pleasure of telling such interesting news, spreading it, and being first to report it carries the story everywhere. This is so well understood that no sensible person pays attention until stronger evidence confirms the report. Do not these same passions, together with still stronger ones, incline most people to believe and report every religious miracle with the greatest fervour and assurance?

94. _Thirdly_, a strong presumption against every supernatural and miraculous account arises from the fact that they abound chiefly among ignorant and barbarous nations. Where a civilized people has accepted them, it will be found to have received them from ignorant and barbarous ancestors. Those ancestors handed them down with the inviolable sanction and authority that always accompany established opinions. Reading the earliest histories of every nation, we may imagine ourselves transported to another world. The entire framework of nature is dislocated, and every element operates differently from the way it does today. Battles, revolutions, pestilence, famine, and death never result from the natural causes familiar to experience. Prodigies, omens, oracles, and judgments completely obscure the few natural events mingled with them. But these wonders become scarcer on every page as we approach more enlightened ages. We soon learn that nothing mysterious or supernatural is involved: everything arises from humanity's ordinary attraction to the marvellous. Though good sense and learning may occasionally check that inclination, it can never be completely rooted out of human nature.

_It is strange_, a discerning reader is apt to say when reading these historians of wonders, _that such prodigious_ _events never happen in our days_. But surely there is nothing strange in people lying in every age. You must have seen enough examples of that weakness. You yourself have heard many marvellous stories begin, only to be abandoned eventually even by ordinary people after the wise and discerning treated them with contempt. Be assured that the celebrated lies which have spread and grown to such monstrous proportions began in just the same way. Planted in more suitable soil, however, they eventually grew into prodigies almost equal to the prodigies they describe.

The false prophet Alexander, now forgotten but once so famous, acted shrewdly when he staged his first impostures in Paphlagonia. As Lucian tells us, its people were extremely ignorant and stupid, ready to swallow even the grossest delusion. Distant people weak enough to think the affair worth investigating at all have no opportunity to obtain better information. A hundred circumstances magnify the stories reaching them. Fools work hard to spread the imposture, while the wise and learned generally content themselves with mocking its absurdity, without learning the specific facts that would clearly refute it. In this way, the impostor advanced from his ignorant Paphlagonians to recruiting followers even among Grecian philosophers and people of the highest rank and distinction in Rome. He even attracted the attention of the wise emperor Marcus Aurelius, to the point that the emperor entrusted the success of a military expedition to his deceptive prophecies.

Beginning an imposture among an ignorant people offers enormous advantages. Even if the delusion is too crude to deceive most of them—_which, though seldom, is sometimes the case_—it stands a much better chance abroad than if it had begun in a city renowned for arts and learning. The most ignorant and barbarous of these barbarians carry the report overseas. None of their countrymen has extensive correspondence or enough standing and authority to contradict and suppress the delusion. People's attraction to the marvellous has full scope. A story universally discredited where it began thus passes as certain a thousand miles away. Had Alexander settled in Athens, however, the philosophers of that famous centre of learning would immediately have spread their judgment of the matter throughout the Roman empire. Supported by such authority and presented with the full force of reason and eloquence, it would have completely opened people's eyes. Admittedly, Lucian happened to pass through Paphlagonia and had the opportunity to perform this service. But, much as we might wish it, not every Alexander encounters a Lucian ready to detect and expose his impostures.

95. I may add a _fourth_ reason for reducing the authority of prodigies. No testimony for any of them—even those never expressly exposed—is free from opposition by an immense number of witnesses. Thus, not only does the miracle undermine the testimony's credibility: the testimony undermines itself. To understand this better, consider that in religion, whatever differs is opposed. The religions of ancient Rome, Turkey, Siam, and China cannot all rest on a solid foundation. Every miracle claimed for any one of these religions—and all abound in miracles—directly aims to establish the particular system to which it belongs. It therefore has the same force, though less directly, towards overthrowing every other system. By destroying a rival system, it also destroys the credibility of the miracles on which that system rests. All the prodigies of different religions must consequently count as conflicting facts, and the evidence for them, strong or weak, as mutually opposed. On this reasoning, when we believe a miracle of Mahomet or his successors, our warrant is the testimony of a few barbarous Arabians. Against them we must set the authority of Titus Livius, Plutarch, Tacitus, and, in short, every Grecian, Chinese, and Roman Catholic author or witness who has reported a miracle in his own religion. We must, I say, treat their testimony exactly as if they had mentioned that Mahometan miracle and explicitly contradicted it, with the same certainty they claim for the miracle they themselves report. This argument may seem excessively subtle and refined. In reality, it is no different from a judge's reasoning when he considers two witnesses accusing someone of a crime discredited by two others who affirm that the accused was two hundred leagues away at the very moment the crime allegedly occurred.

96. Among the best-attested miracles in all secular history is Tacitus's account of Vespasian. In Alexandria, Vespasian cured a blind man with his spittle and a lame man merely by touching him with his foot. The men acted in obedience to a vision of the god Serapis, who had directed them to seek these miraculous cures from the Emperor. The story appears in that fine historian[23], where every circumstance seems to strengthen the testimony. These circumstances could be developed at length with all the force of argument and eloquence, if anyone now cared to defend the evidence for that discredited, idolatrous superstition. Consider the dignity, sound judgment, age, and honesty of so great an emperor. Throughout his life he dealt familiarly with friends and courtiers, never adopting the extraordinary airs of divinity assumed by Alexander and Demetrius. Consider the historian: a contemporary renowned for candour and truthfulness, and perhaps the greatest and most penetrating genius of antiquity. He was so far from credulous that he was accused of the opposite faults, atheism and irreligion. Consider those on whose authority he reported the miracle: people, we may reasonably presume, with established reputations for judgment and truthfulness. They were eyewitnesses who reaffirmed their testimony after the Flavian family had lost the empire and could no longer reward a lie. _Utrumque, qui interfuere, nunc quoque memorant, postquam nullum mendacio pretium_. Add the public character of the reported facts, and we can hardly imagine stronger evidence for so gross and obvious a falsehood.
[23] Hist. lib. iv. cap. 81. Suetonius supplies an almost identical account _in vita_ Vesp.

Cardinal de Retz also tells a memorable story that deserves consideration. Fleeing into Spain to escape persecution by his enemies, that scheming politician passed through Saragossa, the capital of Arragon. In the cathedral he was shown a man who had served as doorkeeper for seven years and was known to everyone in town who had ever worshipped there. For all that time he had been seen without a leg, but he had recovered the limb after holy oil was rubbed on the stump. The cardinal assures us that he saw the man with two legs. Every canon of the church vouched for the miracle, and all the company in town were appealed to for confirmation. Their fervent devotion convinced the cardinal that they thoroughly believed it. Here again, the narrator lived at the time of the supposed prodigy. He was sceptical and libertine in character, as well as exceptionally gifted. The miracle was so _singular_ that it scarcely admitted of counterfeiting; the witnesses were numerous, and virtually all were spectators of the fact they attested. Another circumstance greatly strengthens the evidence and may double our surprise: the cardinal who tells the story seems to disbelieve it himself, and therefore cannot be suspected of joining in the holy fraud. He rightly considered that rejecting such a fact did not require him to disprove the testimony precisely or trace its falsehood through every circumstance of trickery and credulity that produced it. He knew that even a small distance in time or place usually made this impossible, and that even immediate presence made it extremely difficult, because of the bigotry, ignorance, cunning, and dishonesty of much of humanity. Reasoning correctly, he therefore concluded that the evidence carried falsehood on its face, and that a miracle supported by any human testimony was more properly an object of ridicule than of argument.

Surely no individual has ever been credited with more miracles than those recently said to have occurred in France at the tomb of Abbe Paris, the famous Jansenist whose supposed holiness deluded people for so long. Everywhere, people spoke of healing the sick, restoring hearing to the deaf, and giving sight to the blind as the ordinary effects of that holy tomb. More remarkably, many miracles were immediately proved on the spot before judges of unquestioned honesty, through witnesses of standing and distinction, in a learned age and on the world's most prominent stage. Nor was that all. An account was published and circulated everywhere. The _Jesuits_, despite being a learned body supported by the civil magistrate and determined enemies of the opinions supposedly favoured by the miracles, could never clearly refute or expose them[24]. Where else shall we find so many circumstances converging to confirm one fact? What can we set against such a cloud of witnesses except the absolute impossibility, or miraculous character, of the events they report? Surely every reasonable person will regard that alone as a sufficient refutation.

[24] The author of this book was Mons. Montgeron, a counsellor or judge in the parliament of Paris, and a man of standing and character. He also became a martyr to the cause and is now said to be held somewhere in a dungeon because of his book.

Another book, in three volumes, called _Recueil des Miracles de l'Abbe_ Paris, describes many of these miracles and includes very well-written introductory discourses. Yet throughout these runs an absurd comparison between our Saviour's miracles and the Abbe's, claiming that the evidence for the latter equals the evidence for the former. As though human testimony could ever be weighed against the testimony of God himself, who guided the inspired writers' pens! If we did treat those writers merely as human witnesses, the French author would be very restrained in his comparison. He might claim, with some appearance of reason, that the Jansenist miracles far exceed the others in evidence and authority. The following details come from authentic documents included in the book just mentioned.

Many miracles attributed to Abbe Paris were immediately established through witnesses before the officiality, or bishop's court, in Paris. This took place under cardinal Noailles's supervision; even his enemies never challenged his reputation for honesty and ability.

His successor as archbishop opposed the Jansenists and was appointed to the see by the court for that reason. Nevertheless, 22 rectors or cures of Paris pressed him with immense earnestness to investigate the miracles. They declared them known to the whole world and indisputably certain. He wisely refrained.

The Molinist party tried to discredit these miracles in one case, that of Mademoiselle le Franc. Their proceedings were extraordinarily irregular in many respects, especially in calling only a few Jansenist witnesses and tampering with them. Beyond that, they soon found themselves overwhelmed by a host of new witnesses: one hundred and twenty, mostly people of standing and means in Paris, who swore to the miracle. A solemn and urgent appeal to parliament accompanied this testimony. The authorities, however, forbade parliament to interfere. Eventually it was observed that when zeal and enthusiasm inflame people, testimony of any conceivable strength can be obtained for the greatest absurdity. Those foolish enough to investigate through that medium, searching for particular defects in testimony, are almost certain to be confounded. An imposture must be very poor indeed if it cannot win that contest.

Anyone who was in France around that time heard of Mons. Heraut, the _lieutenant de Police_. His vigilance, insight, energy, and extensive intelligence were widely discussed. This magistrate, whose office made him almost absolute, received full powers specifically to suppress or discredit these miracles. He frequently seized and immediately examined both the witnesses and the people concerned. Yet he could never obtain satisfactory evidence against them.

In Mademoiselle Thibaut's case, he sent the famous De Sylva to examine her. The physician's evidence is very curious. He declared that she could not possibly have been as ill as the witnesses proved, since she could not possibly have recovered in so short a time as completely as he found her. Like a sensible man, he reasoned from natural causes. The other party replied that the whole affair was a miracle, and that his evidence was the best possible proof of it.

The Molinists faced a painful dilemma. They dared not claim that human evidence was wholly insufficient to prove a miracle. They had to say that witchcraft and the devil had produced these miracles. Their opponents replied that this was the same recourse taken by the Jews of old.

No Jansenist had difficulty explaining why the miracles stopped when the king's decree closed the churchyard. Touching the tomb produced these extraordinary effects; when nobody could approach it, no effects could be expected. God could indeed have knocked down the walls in an instant, but he is master of his own graces and works, and it is not for us to explain them. He did not bring down every city's walls at the sound of rams' horns, as he did at Jericho, nor open every apostle's prison as he opened St. Paul's.

No less a person than the Due de Chatillon, a duke and peer of France of the highest rank and family, testified to a miraculous cure performed on his servant. The servant had lived in his house for several years with a visible and tangible infirmity. I shall conclude by observing that no clergy are more renowned for strictness of life and manners than France's secular clergy, particularly the rectors or cures of Paris who testify to these impostures. Throughout Europe, the learning, genius, and honesty of the gentlemen of Port-Royal, and the austerity of its nuns, have been celebrated. Yet they all testify to a miracle performed on the niece of the famous Pascal, whose holiness of life and extraordinary ability are well known. The famous Racine describes this miracle in his celebrated history of Port-Royal. He supports it with every proof that a multitude of nuns, priests, physicians, and people of the world, all of unquestioned credibility, could supply. Several learned men, particularly the bishop of Tournay, considered the miracle so certain that they used it to refute atheists and free-thinkers. France's queen-regent, strongly prejudiced against Port-Royal, sent her own physician to investigate; he returned completely convinced. In short, the supernatural cure was so indisputable that for a time it saved that famous monastery from the destruction threatened by the Jesuits. Had it been a fraud, such perceptive and powerful opponents would certainly have exposed it, hastening its authors' ruin. Our divines can build a formidable castle from contemptible materials: what a prodigious structure they could have raised from these circumstances and many others I have omitted! How often the great names of Pascal, Racine, Amaud, and Nicole would have rung in our ears! If wise, however, they had better adopt this miracle: it is worth a thousand times more than all the rest of the collection. Besides, it may suit their purposes very well. For this miracle really was performed by touching an authentic holy prickle of the holy thorn that formed the holy crown, which, and so on.

97. Some human testimony carries the greatest force and authority in certain cases—for example, when it reports the battle of Philippi or Pharsalia. Does it follow that every kind of testimony must have equal force and authority in every case? Suppose the Caesarean and Pompeian factions had each claimed victory in those battles, and each party's historians had consistently assigned the advantage to their own side. How could people at this distance have decided between them? The conflict is equally strong between miracles reported by Herodotus or Plutarch and those recounted by Mariana, Bede, or any monastic historian.

The wise give a very sceptical, academic assent to any report that favours the reporter's passions—whether it glorifies his country, his family, or himself, or otherwise suits his natural inclinations and tendencies. But what temptation could be greater than appearing as a missionary, a prophet, an ambassador from heaven? Who would not face many dangers and difficulties to attain so exalted a character? Or suppose vanity and a heated imagination have first converted the man himself, and he has sincerely embraced the delusion. Who then hesitates to use pious frauds in support of so holy and meritorious a cause?

Here the smallest spark can grow into the greatest blaze, because the fuel is always ready. The _avidum genus auricularum_[25], the gaping populace, eagerly accept without examination whatever gratifies superstition and encourages wonder.
[25] Lucret.

How many stories of this kind have been exposed and discredited in their infancy in every age? How many more enjoyed a period of fame before sinking into neglect and oblivion? When such reports circulate, the explanation is therefore obvious. We judge in accordance with regular experience and observation when we account for them through the familiar, natural principles of credulity and delusion. Shall we reject so natural an explanation and instead accept a miraculous violation of nature's most firmly established laws?

I need hardly mention how difficult it is to uncover a falsehood in any private or even public history at the very place where the event supposedly happened. The difficulty grows when the scene is even slightly distant. Even a court of law, with all the authority, precision, and judgment it can employ, often struggles to distinguish truth from falsehood in the most recent events. The matter never reaches a resolution if left to the ordinary process of quarrelling, debate, and circulating rumours—especially when people's passions have become involved on either side.

When a religion is new, the wise and learned usually consider it too insignificant to deserve their attention. Later, when they wish to expose the fraud and free the deluded multitude from error, the opportunity has passed. The records and witnesses that might have settled the matter are irretrievably lost.

No means of exposure then remain except those drawn from the reporters' own testimony. Although these always suffice for discerning and knowledgeable people, they are usually too subtle for ordinary people to grasp.

98. Taken together, these considerations show that testimony for a miracle of any kind has never amounted even to probability, much less to proof. Even supposing it did amount to proof, another proof would oppose it, drawn from the very nature of the fact it sought to establish. Experience alone gives human testimony its authority, and that same experience assures us of nature's laws. When these two kinds of experience conflict, we can only subtract one from the other and adopt an opinion on either side with the assurance supplied by the remainder. But under the principle explained here, this subtraction entirely cancels the evidence in the case of every popular religion. We may therefore establish this rule: no human testimony can be strong enough to prove a miracle and make it a sound foundation for any such religious system.

99. Please notice the limitations I place on the claim when I say that a miracle can never be proved so as to found a system of religion. Outside that case, I admit there may possibly be miracles, or violations of nature's usual course, of a kind that human testimony could prove, though perhaps no example can be found in all historical records. Suppose, for instance, that all authors in every language agreed that from the first of January 1600, complete darkness covered the whole earth for eight days. Suppose the tradition of this extraordinary event remained strong and vivid among the people, and every traveller returning from abroad reported the same tradition without the slightest variation or contradiction. Clearly, present-day philosophers should accept the fact as certain rather than doubt it, and should search for its possible causes. So many analogies make nature's decay, corruption, and dissolution probable that any phenomenon appearing to tend towards that catastrophe falls within the reach of human testimony, provided that testimony is very widespread and uniform.

But suppose all historians of England agreed that Queen Elizabeth died on the first of January 1600. Suppose they agreed that, as is usual for someone of her rank, her physicians and the whole court saw her before and after death; that parliament acknowledged and proclaimed her successor; and that after a month in the grave she reappeared, reclaimed the throne, and governed England for three years. I confess that this combination of strange circumstances would surprise me, but I would feel no inclination whatever to believe so miraculous an event. I would not doubt her pretended death or the other public circumstances following it. I would merely insist that the death was pretended, neither real nor possibly real. You might object that deceiving the world in so important an affair would be difficult, almost impossible; that the renowned queen was wise and sound in judgment; and that so paltry a trick could bring her little or no advantage. Your objections would be vain. All this might astonish me, but I would still reply that human dishonesty and folly are so common that I would rather believe their combination produced the most extraordinary events than accept so striking a violation of nature's laws.

Now suppose this miracle were attributed to a new religious system. In every age people have been deceived so often by ridiculous stories of this kind that this circumstance alone would fully prove a fraud. It would be enough for every sensible person to reject the fact, and even to reject it without further investigation. Although the Being credited with the miracle is Almighty, that does not make it any more probable. We cannot know the attributes or actions of such a Being except through our experience of his productions in nature's ordinary course. We are therefore still confined to past observation. To judge which is likelier, we must compare instances of truth being violated in human testimony with instances of nature's laws being violated by miracles. Since falsehood is more common in testimony about religious miracles than in testimony about any other matter of fact, this must greatly weaken the former's authority. It must lead us to resolve generally never to give it attention, whatever plausible pretence may cover it.

Lord Bacon seems to have adopted the same principles of reasoning. 'We ought,' says he, 'to make a collection or particular history of all monsters and prodigious births or productions, and in a word of every thing new, rare, and extraordinary in nature. But this must be done with the most severe scrutiny, lest we depart from truth. Above all, every relation must be considered as suspicious, which depends in any degree upon religion, as the prodigies of Livy: And no less so, every thing that is to be found in the writers of natural magic or alchimy, or such authors, who seem, all of them, to have an unconquerable appetite for falsehood and fable[26].'
[26] Nov. Org. lib. ii. aph. 29.

100. I am all the more pleased with the reasoning presented here because I think it may confound those dangerous friends, or disguised enemies, of the _Christian Religion_ who undertake to defend it through human reason. Our most holy religion rests on _Faith_, not reason. Exposing it to a trial it is in no way equipped to endure is a sure way of exposing its weakness. To make this clearer, let us examine the miracles reported in scripture. Rather than lose ourselves in too vast a field, let us restrict ourselves to the _Pentateuch_. Following the principles of these pretended Christians, we shall examine it as the work of a merely human writer and historian, rather than as God's own word or testimony. We must first consider a book presented to us by an ignorant and barbarous people, written when they were still more barbarous, and probably long after the events it describes. No supporting testimony confirms it, and it resembles the fabulous accounts every nation gives of its origins. Reading it, we find it filled with prodigies and miracles. It describes a condition of the world and human nature entirely different from the present; our fall from that condition; human lifespans approaching a thousand years; the world's destruction by a flood; the arbitrary selection of one people as heaven's favourites—and those people the author's own countrymen; and their release from bondage through the most astonishing prodigies imaginable. Let anyone put his hand on his heart and, after serious reflection, declare whether he thinks the falsehood of such a book, supported by such testimony, would be more extraordinary and miraculous than all the miracles it reports. Yet the measures of probability established above require precisely that before we can accept it.

101. Everything we have said about miracles applies without alteration to prophecies. Indeed, every prophecy is a real miracle, and only as such can it count as proof of revelation. If predicting future events did not exceed human nature's capacity, using a prophecy as evidence of a divine mission or heavenly authority would be absurd. We may therefore conclude, taking the matter as a whole, that the _Christian Religion_ was not merely accompanied by miracles at its beginning: even today, no reasonable person can believe it without one. Reason alone cannot convince us of its truth. Whoever is moved by _Faith_ to accept it is conscious of a continuing miracle within himself, one that overturns every principle of his understanding and determines him to believe what most contradicts custom and experience.

chapters.title: Section 11: OF A PARTICULAR PROVIDENCE AND OF A FUTURE STATE.
paragraphs: 102. Recently I had a conversation with a friend who enjoys sceptical paradoxes. He advanced many principles I cannot approve of at all. Yet they seem interesting, and connected in some way with the reasoning developed throughout this enquiry. I shall therefore reproduce them here from memory as accurately as I can, so that the reader may judge them.

Our conversation began with my admiration for philosophy's exceptional good fortune. More than any other privilege, philosophy requires complete liberty, and it flourishes chiefly through free disagreement and argument. It first arose in an age and country of freedom and toleration, where no creeds, concessions, or penal laws restricted even its most extravagant principles. Apart from Protagoras's banishment and Socrates's death—the latter partly caused by other motives—ancient history offers scarcely any examples of the bigoted suspicion that so plagues the present age. Epicurus lived peacefully and quietly in Athens to an advanced age. Epicureans[27] were even permitted to become priests and officiate at the altar in the established religion's most sacred rites. The wisest of all Roman emperors[29] provided public encouragement through pensions and salaries[28] equally to teachers of every philosophical school. We can easily understand how necessary such treatment was in philosophy's youth. Even now, when we might suppose her tougher and stronger, she struggles to endure the harsh seasons and the bitter winds of slander and persecution blowing against her.
[27] Luciani [Greek: symp. ae Lapithai].
[28] Luciani [Greek: eunouchos].
[29] Luciani and Dio.

You admire as philosophy's exceptional good fortune, my friend said, what seems to follow naturally from the course of things, and to be inevitable in every age and nation. The stubborn bigotry you complain of as so destructive to philosophy is actually her own offspring. After joining forces with superstition, it abandons its parent's interests entirely and becomes her most determined enemy and persecutor. The speculative religious dogmas that now provoke such furious disputes could not have been conceived or accepted in the world's early ages. Wholly uneducated people formed a conception of religion better suited to their weak understanding. Their sacred doctrines consisted chiefly of stories accepted through tradition rather than argument or debate. Once the initial alarm over the philosophers' new paradoxes and principles had passed, these teachers seem to have lived harmoniously with established superstition throughout antiquity. Between them they made an equitable division of humanity: philosophy claimed the learned and wise, while superstition retained the common and uneducated.
