103. It seems, then, I said, that you leave politics out altogether. You never suppose that a wise magistrate might rightly distrust certain philosophical doctrines, such as those of Epicurus. By denying divine existence, and consequently providence and a future state, they seem greatly to loosen morality's bonds, and may therefore be thought harmful to the peace of civil society.

I know, he replied, that in no age have these persecutions actually arisen from calm reasoning or experience of philosophy's harmful consequences. They have sprung entirely from passion and prejudice. But suppose I went further and claimed that, had one of those days' _sycophants_ or informers accused Epicurus before the people, he could easily have defended himself. He could have proved his philosophical principles as beneficial as those of the opponents who so zealously tried to expose him to public hatred and suspicion.

I wish, I said, that you would try your eloquence on so extraordinary a subject. Give a speech for Epicurus that might satisfy, if not the Athenian mob—assuming you allow that ancient and cultivated city to have contained a mob—the more philosophical members of his audience, whom we may suppose capable of understanding his arguments.

On those terms, he replied, the task would not be difficult. If you like, I shall become Epicurus for a moment and let you represent the Athenian people. I shall deliver a speech that fills the entire voting urn with white beans, leaving not a single black one to gratify my opponents' malice.
Very well: please go ahead on those assumptions.

104. I come before your assembly, O Athenians, to justify what I taught in my school. Instead of reasoning with calm and impartial inquirers, I find myself accused by furious opponents. Your deliberations ought rightly to concern the public good and the commonwealth's interests. Instead, they are diverted into speculative philosophy's investigations. These magnificent but perhaps fruitless inquiries displace your more familiar and more useful occupations. So far as I can, I shall prevent this abuse. We shall not debate here the origin and government of worlds. We shall ask only how far such questions affect the public interest. If I can persuade you that they have no bearing on society's peace or government's security, I hope you will promptly send us back to our schools. There we may examine at leisure the most sublime, but also the most speculative, question in all philosophy.

Religious philosophers are not content with your forefathers' traditions and your priests' teachings, which I willingly accept. With rash curiosity, they try to discover how far reason can establish religion. In doing so, they provoke rather than resolve the doubts that careful, searching inquiry naturally raises. They paint the universe's order, beauty, and wise arrangement in the most magnificent colours. Then they ask whether so glorious a display of intelligence could arise from atoms coming together by chance, or whether chance could produce what even the greatest genius can never sufficiently admire. I shall not examine whether this argument is sound. I shall grant it every strength my opponents and accusers could desire. It will be enough if, through this very reasoning, I can prove that the question is entirely speculative. In denying providence and a future state in my philosophical inquiries, I do not undermine society's foundations. I advance principles that my opponents themselves, reasoning consistently from their own arguments, must accept as sound and satisfactory.

105. You, my accusers, have acknowledged that the chief or sole argument for divine existence—which I have never questioned—comes from nature's order. You see such signs of intelligence and design there that you consider it extravagant to attribute them either to chance or to matter's blind, unguided force. You admit that this argument proceeds from effects to causes. From the work's orderly arrangement you infer planning and foresight in the worker. You acknowledge that unless you establish this point, your conclusion fails. Nor do you claim to establish a broader conclusion than nature's phenomena justify. These are your concessions. I ask you to observe what follows from them.

When we infer a particular cause from an effect, we must keep the two in proportion. We may attribute to the cause only those qualities exactly sufficient to produce the effect. A ten-ounce body rising in a balance may prove that the opposing weight exceeds ten ounces, but cannot give us any reason to say it exceeds a hundred. If the cause assigned to an effect cannot produce it, we must reject that cause or add qualities that make it properly proportionate to the effect. But if we attribute further qualities to it, or declare it capable of producing other effects, we are merely indulging in free conjecture. We arbitrarily assume qualities and powers exist without any reason or authority.

The same rule applies whether the proposed cause is brute, unconscious matter or a rational, intelligent being. If we know the cause only through its effect, we should never attribute qualities to it beyond those precisely needed to produce that effect. Nor does sound reasoning permit us to work back from the cause and infer additional effects beyond those through which alone we know it. Merely seeing a picture by Zeuxis could not tell anyone that he was also a sculptor or architect, as skilful with stone and marble as with colours. We can safely conclude that the artist possessed the abilities and taste displayed in the particular work before us. The cause must match the effect. If we match them exactly and precisely, we shall never find qualities in the cause that point beyond it or support an inference about another design or performance. Such qualities would exceed what is merely needed to produce the effect we are examining.

106. Grant, then, that the gods created the universe or gave it order. It follows that they possess precisely the degree of power, intelligence, and benevolence visible in their work. Nothing further can ever be proved unless we use exaggeration and flattery to fill the gaps in argument and reasoning. Wherever traces of an attribute now appear, we may conclude that the attribute exists to that extent. Supposing further attributes is mere hypothesis. Still more hypothetical is the supposition that distant regions of space or periods of time have seen, or will see, a more magnificent display of those attributes, with a system of government better suited to these imagined virtues. We may never ascend from the universe, the effect, to Jupiter, the cause, and then descend again to infer a new effect from that cause—as if the present effects alone were not fully worthy of the glorious attributes we assign to that deity. Since knowledge of the cause comes solely from the effect, the two must correspond exactly. The cause can point to nothing further or support any new inference and conclusion.

You observe certain phenomena in nature. You look for a cause or author and imagine you have found him. Then you fall so deeply in love with this creation of your own mind that you think he must produce something greater and more perfect than the present scene, so full of evil and disorder. You forget that this supreme intelligence and benevolence are entirely imaginary, or at least unsupported by reason. You have no grounds to attribute any qualities to him except those you see him actually exercise and display in his productions. Let your gods, then, O philosophers, fit nature's present appearances. Do not presume to alter those appearances through arbitrary suppositions so that they fit the attributes you so fondly assign to your deities.

107. When priests and poets, supported by your authority, O Athenians, speak of a golden or silver age preceding the present condition of vice and misery, I listen attentively and reverently. But when philosophers who claim to disregard authority and cultivate reason say the same things, I confess that I do not show them the same obedient submission and pious deference. I ask who carried them into heaven, admitted them to the gods' councils, or opened the book of fate to them. How else can they so rashly assert that their deities have accomplished, or will accomplish, some purpose beyond what has actually appeared? If they say they climbed reason's steps, ascending gradually by inference from effects to causes, I still insist that imagination's wings helped reason climb. Otherwise they could not change their method of inference and argue from causes to effects. They presume that a more perfect creation than this world would better suit beings as perfect as the gods, forgetting that they have no reason to assign these heavenly beings any perfection or attribute beyond what can be found in the present world.

Hence all the fruitless labour spent explaining nature's evil appearances and saving the gods' honour, while we must acknowledge the reality of the evil and disorder abounding in the world. We are told that matter's stubborn and unmanageable qualities, or the observance of general laws, or some similar reason alone restricted Jupiter's power and benevolence. This forced him to make humanity and every sentient creature so imperfect and unhappy. His attributes, then, are apparently taken for granted beforehand in their fullest extent. On that assumption, I admit these conjectures might be accepted as plausible explanations of the evil phenomena. But I still ask: why take the attributes for granted? Why assign the cause any qualities beyond those actually appearing in the effect? Why torment your brain to justify nature's course through suppositions that, for all you know, may be entirely imaginary, and of which nature's course reveals no trace?

The religious hypothesis must therefore be treated only as one particular way of explaining the universe's visible phenomena. No sound reasoner will presume to infer a single new fact from it, or alter or add to those phenomena in any detail. If you think the appearances of things prove such causes, you may infer that those causes exist. Everyone should enjoy freedom to conjecture and argue on subjects so complex and sublime. But there you should stop. Suppose you reverse direction and argue from your inferred causes, concluding that some additional fact has occurred or will occur in nature's course to display particular attributes more fully. I must warn you that you have abandoned the method of reasoning appropriate to this subject. You have certainly added something to the cause's attributes beyond what appears in the effect. Otherwise, you could never add anything to the effect to make it more worthy of the cause with even tolerable sense or propriety.

108. Where, then, is the offensiveness of the doctrine I teach in my school—or, rather, examine in my gardens? What do you find anywhere in this question that concerns, even slightly, the preservation of good morals or society's peace and order?

You say I deny providence and a supreme governor of the world who directs events, punishes the vicious with disgrace and disappointment, and rewards the virtuous with honour and success in all their undertakings. But I certainly do not deny the course of events itself, which lies open to everyone's inquiry and examination. I acknowledge that under the present arrangement of things, virtue brings more peace of mind than vice and receives a more favourable welcome from the world. I recognize that humanity's past experience makes friendship the chief joy of human life and moderation the only source of tranquillity and happiness. I never hesitate between a virtuous and a vicious life. I know that for a well-disposed mind every advantage lies with the former. Granting all your suppositions and arguments, what more can you say? You tell me, indeed, that intelligence and design produce this arrangement. But whatever produces it, the arrangement itself remains unchanged. Our happiness or misery depends on it, and consequently so does our conduct in life. I remain as free as you to guide my behaviour by experience of past events. Suppose you say that once divine providence and supreme distributive justice in the universe are admitted, I should expect some more particular reward for the good and punishment for the bad beyond the ordinary course of events. I find here the same fallacy I have already tried to expose. You continue to imagine that if we grant the divine existence you so earnestly defend, you can safely infer consequences from it. Arguing from the attributes you give your gods, you add something to nature's experienced order. You seem to forget that all your reasoning here can proceed only from effects to causes. Every argument from causes to effects must necessarily be a gross sophism, because you can know nothing of the cause except what you have already, not inferred, but fully discovered in the effect.

109. What, then, must a philosopher think of those vain reasoners who refuse to make the present scene their sole object of contemplation? They reverse nature's entire course, making this life merely a passage to something beyond it: a porch leading to a greater and vastly different building, or a prologue serving only to introduce the play and lend it grace and appropriateness. Where do you suppose these philosophers get their idea of the gods? Surely from their own fancy and imagination. If they derived it from present phenomena, it could never point further, but would have to fit those phenomena exactly. We may freely admit that the divinity could _possibly_ possess attributes we have never seen exercised, or be governed by principles of action whose fulfilment we cannot discover. Yet this remains mere _possibility_ and hypothesis. We can never have reason to _infer_ attributes or principles of action in him beyond the extent to which we know they have been exercised and fulfilled.

_Are there any marks of a distributive justice in the world?_ If you say yes, I conclude that since justice operates here, it is satisfied here. If you say no, I conclude that you have no reason to attribute justice, in our sense of the word, to the gods. If you take a middle position and say that divine justice currently operates in part but not to its fullest extent, I reply that you have no reason to assign it any particular extent beyond the one in which you see it operating _at present_.

110. Thus, O Athenians, I bring my dispute with my opponents to a brief conclusion. Nature's course lies as open to my contemplation as to theirs. The sequence of events we experience is the great standard by which we all guide our conduct. Nothing else can be appealed to in the field or senate; nothing else should ever be heard of in the school or private study. Our limited understanding would struggle in vain to cross these boundaries, however narrow our eager imagination finds them. When we argue from nature's course to a particular intelligent cause that first gave the universe order and still preserves it, we adopt a principle both uncertain and useless. It is uncertain because its subject lies entirely beyond human experience. It is useless because our knowledge of this cause comes entirely from nature's course. Under the rules of sound reasoning, we cannot return from the cause with a new inference, add to nature's ordinary and experienced course, or establish new principles of conduct and behaviour.

111. I see, I said when he finished his speech, that you have not neglected the tricks of the ancient demagogues. Since you chose to make me represent the people, you seek my favour by adopting principles you know I have always particularly cherished. I grant that you make experience the sole standard of our judgment on this and every other question of fact—as indeed I think you should. Yet I have no doubt that the very experience you appeal to may refute the reasoning you have put in Epicurus's mouth. Suppose, for example, you saw a half-finished building surrounded by heaps of bricks, stone, and mortar, together with all the mason's tools. Could you not _infer_ from the effect that design and planning produced it? Could you not then return from this inferred cause to infer additions to the effect, concluding that the building would soon be completed and receive every further improvement skill could give it? If you saw a human footprint on the shore, you would conclude that someone had passed that way and had also left the other foot's print, although shifting sand or flooding water had erased it. Why refuse the same reasoning about nature's order? Treat the world and present life simply as an unfinished building, from which you infer a superior intelligence. Then, reasoning from that intelligence, which can leave nothing imperfect, why not infer a more finished scheme or plan to be completed at some distant point in space or time? Are these methods of reasoning not exactly alike? On what grounds can you accept one while rejecting the other?

112. The infinite difference between the subjects, he replied, sufficiently grounds the difference between my conclusions. With works of _human_ skill and planning, we may move from effect to cause, then return from cause to draw new inferences about the effect and examine changes it probably has undergone or may yet undergo. But what supports this reasoning? Plainly, it is that we know human beings through experience. We know their motives and plans, and their projects and inclinations have a certain connection and coherence under the laws nature has established for governing such creatures. When we discover that human skill and labour produced a work, our independent knowledge of the animal's nature allows a hundred inferences about what to expect from it. Every inference rests on experience and observation. But if we knew humanity only through the single work or production being examined, we could not reason this way. All our knowledge of the qualities we assign to the maker would then come from that production. Those qualities could point no further and could support no new inference. Considered alone, a footprint in sand proves only that something with a matching shape produced it. But a human footprint also proves, through our other experience, that there was probably another foot, which likewise left a print later erased by time or some other accident. Here we rise from effect to cause and descend again to infer changes in the effect. Yet this is not simply the continuation of one chain of reasoning. We include a hundred other experiences and observations about the _usual_ shape and limbs of that animal species. Without them, this method of argument would be fallacious and sophistical.

113. Reasoning from nature's works is different. We know the Deity only through his productions. He is a unique being in the universe, belonging to no species or genus whose experienced attributes or qualities could let us infer his attributes or qualities by analogy. The universe displays wisdom and goodness, so we infer wisdom and goodness. It displays a particular degree of these perfections, so we infer precisely that degree, fitted exactly to the effect we examine. No rules of sound reasoning authorize us to infer or suppose further attributes, or higher degrees of the same attributes. Without taking some such liberty in our suppositions, we cannot argue from the cause or infer any change in the effect beyond what we have directly observed. Greater good produced by this Being must demonstrate greater goodness. A fairer distribution of rewards and punishments must arise from greater regard for justice and equity. Every imagined addition to nature's works adds to the attributes of nature's Author. Entirely unsupported by reason or argument, it can therefore be admitted only as conjecture and hypothesis[30].

[30] I think we may establish this general rule: when a cause is known only through its particular effects, no new effects can be inferred from it. The qualities needed to produce these new effects alongside the earlier ones must differ from, exceed, or operate more widely than the qualities that merely produced the effect through which alone we supposedly know the cause. We can therefore have no reason to suppose such qualities exist. The difficulty remains if we say that the new effects arise merely from the continuation of the same energy already known through the first effects. Even granting this—which can seldom be supposed—the very continuation and exercise of a similar energy is an arbitrary supposition. It cannot be absolutely the same energy. Exercising a similar energy, I say, at a different point in space and time is a supposition of which no trace can possibly appear in the effects from which all our knowledge of the cause originally comes. Let the _inferred_ cause be proportioned exactly, as it should be, to the known effect. It cannot then possess qualities from which new or different effects may be _inferred_.

The chief source of our mistake here, and of the unlimited conjecture we allow ourselves, is that we silently put ourselves in the Supreme Being's place. We conclude that on every occasion he will act as we would consider reasonable and desirable in his position. But nature's ordinary course may already convince us that almost everything follows principles and rules very different from ours. Beyond that, reasoning from human intentions and projects to those of a Being so different and superior plainly violates every rule of analogy. Experience shows a certain coherence between human designs and inclinations. Once a fact reveals one of a person's intentions, experience may often justify inferring another and drawing a long chain of conclusions about his past or future conduct. But this method can never apply to a Being so remote and incomprehensible. He bears far less resemblance to any other being in the universe than the sun bears to a wax candle, and reveals himself only through faint traces or outlines. Beyond these we have no authority to assign him any attribute or perfection. What we imagine a higher perfection may actually be a defect. Even if it were the greatest perfection, attributing it to the Supreme Being when his works do not show it fully exercised suggests flattery and praise more than sound reasoning and philosophy. All the philosophy in the world, then, and all religion insofar as it is merely a kind of philosophy, can never take us beyond experience's ordinary course. They cannot give us rules of conduct and behaviour different from those supplied by reflection on everyday life. The religious hypothesis allows no new fact to be inferred, no event to be foreseen or predicted, no reward to be expected or punishment feared beyond what practice and observation already teach. My defence of Epicurus therefore remains sound and satisfactory. Society's political interests have no connection with philosophical disputes over metaphysics and religion.

114. There is still one circumstance you seem to have missed, I replied. Even if I accepted your premises, I must reject your conclusion. You conclude that religious doctrines and arguments _can_ have no influence on life because they _ought_ to have none. You overlook the fact that people do not reason as you do. They draw many consequences from believing in divine Existence, supposing the Deity will punish vice and reward virtue beyond what appears in nature's ordinary course. Whether their reasoning is sound makes no difference: its influence on their lives and conduct remains the same. For all I know, those who try to free them from such prejudices may be good reasoners. But I cannot count them good citizens or politicians. They remove one restraint on people's passions and, in one respect, make violating society's laws easier and safer.

After all, I may agree with your general conclusion in favour of liberty, though on different premises from the ones you use to support it. I think the state should tolerate every philosophical principle. No instance exists of a government's political interests suffering from such tolerance. Philosophers are not enthusiasts, and their doctrines hold little attraction for the people. Their reasoning cannot be restrained without dangerous consequences for the sciences and even for the state, since this paves the way for persecution and oppression on questions that concern most people more deeply.

115. But, I continued, a difficulty about your main argument occurs to me. I shall simply put it before you without pressing it, lest it lead to reasoning too subtle and delicate. In short, I seriously doubt that a cause can be known only through its effect, as you have assumed throughout, or that it can be so unique and particular as to resemble no other cause or object ever observed. We can infer one object from another only when two _species_ of objects have been found constantly conjoined. If an effect were entirely unique and belonged to no known _species_, I cannot see how we could form any conjecture or inference whatever about its cause. If experience, observation, and analogy really are the only guides we can reasonably follow in such inferences, both effect and cause must resemble other effects and causes we know and have repeatedly found conjoined. I leave you to reflect on this principle's consequences. I shall only observe that Epicurus's opponents always suppose the universe, an entirely unique and unparalleled effect, proves a Deity, a cause equally unique and unparalleled. On that supposition, your reasoning at least seems worthy of our attention. I admit there is some difficulty in seeing how we can ever return from cause to effect and, reasoning from our ideas of the cause, infer any change or addition to the effect.

chapters.title: Section 12: OF THE ACADEMICAL OR SCEPTICAL PHILOSOPHY. — Part 1
paragraphs: 116. No subject has attracted more philosophical arguments than the existence of a Deity and the refutation of _Atheists'_ fallacies. Yet the most religious philosophers still debate whether anyone can be blind enough to be an atheist in theory. How can we reconcile these contradictions? The knights-errant who roamed about ridding the world of dragons and giants never felt the slightest doubt that these monsters existed.

The _Sceptic_ is another enemy of religion who naturally arouses the indignation of every divine and serious philosopher. Yet certainly nobody has ever met such an absurd creature, or spoken with someone who held no opinion or principle on any question of conduct or speculation. This raises a very natural question: what do we mean by a sceptic? And how far can these philosophical principles of doubt and uncertainty be carried?

There is a kind of scepticism _antecedent_ to all study and philosophy, strongly recommended by Des Cartes and others as the supreme safeguard against error and hasty judgment. It recommends doubting everything: not just our previous opinions and principles, but even our own faculties. Their trustworthiness, its advocates say, must be established through a chain of reasoning from some original principle incapable of misleading or deceiving us. But no such original principle has priority over all the other self-evident and convincing principles. Even if one did, we could not move a step beyond it without using the very faculties we are already supposed to distrust. Cartesian doubt, therefore, would be incurable if any human being could ever attain it—which plainly no one can. No reasoning could ever restore assurance and conviction about any subject.

We must admit, however, that in a milder form this kind of scepticism can have a very reasonable meaning. It is a necessary preparation for philosophy, preserving proper impartiality in our judgments and freeing our minds from prejudices absorbed through education or rash opinion. We should begin with clear, self-evident principles, advance by cautious and secure steps, review our conclusions often, and examine all their consequences carefully. Such methods will make our systems develop slowly and take us only a short distance. Yet they are the only methods through which we can ever hope to reach truth and give our judgments proper stability and certainty.

117. Another kind of scepticism is _consequent_ on science and inquiry. Here people supposedly discover either that their mental faculties are entirely deceptive or that they cannot reach any settled conclusion on the intricate speculative subjects they usually investigate. Certain philosophers question even our senses. They subject the rules of ordinary life to the same doubt as the deepest principles or conclusions of metaphysics and theology. We encounter these paradoxical doctrines—if doctrines they can be called—in some philosophers, and their refutation in several others. They naturally awaken our curiosity and lead us to investigate the arguments on which they may rest.

I need not dwell on the familiar arguments sceptics in every age have used against the evidence of _sense_. They point to the countless occasions when our organs are imperfect and misleading: an oar looking bent in water; objects looking different at different distances; double images produced by pressing one eye; and many similar appearances. These sceptical arguments really prove only that we should not trust the senses alone without question. To make them proper _criteria_ of truth and falsehood within their own sphere, we must correct their evidence through reason. We must consider the nature of the medium, the object's distance, and the condition of the organ. Other, deeper arguments against the senses are not so easily answered.

118. A natural instinct or predisposition evidently leads people to trust their senses. Without reasoning, and almost before we can reason, we always assume an external universe independent of our perception. We suppose it would exist even if we and every sentient creature were absent or annihilated. Animals too are governed by a similar opinion. Throughout their thoughts, plans, and actions, they preserve this belief in external objects.

It also seems clear that when people follow this blind, powerful natural instinct, they always take the very images presented by their senses to be the external objects themselves. They never suspect that the former merely represent the latter. We believe this very table, which looks white and feels hard, exists independently of our perception and outside the mind perceiving it. Our presence does not bring it into being, nor does our absence destroy it. Its existence remains complete and unchanged, regardless of the situation of the intelligent beings who perceive or contemplate it.

Yet the slightest philosophy soon destroys this universal, original human opinion. It teaches us that nothing can be present to the mind except an image or perception. The senses are only the channels through which these images enter; they cannot establish direct contact between mind and object. The table we see seems smaller as we move away, but the real table, existing independently of us, does not change. Only its image, therefore, was present to the mind. These are reason's plain conclusions. No reflective person has ever doubted that the things we consider when saying _this house_ and _that tree_ are merely perceptions in the mind: fleeting copies or representations of other things that remain unchanged and independent.

119. Reasoning thus forces us to contradict or depart from nature's original instincts and accept a new account of our senses' evidence. But philosophy finds herself in great difficulty when she tries to justify this account and answer the sceptics' objections and quibbles. She can no longer invoke nature's infallible, irresistible instinct. That instinct led to a quite different account, now acknowledged as fallible and even mistaken. And justifying this supposedly philosophical account through a chain of clear, convincing arguments—or even through something resembling an argument—exceeds the whole capacity of humanity.

What argument can prove that the mind's perceptions must be caused by external objects that are entirely different from them, although resembling them, if that is possible? Why could those perceptions not arise from the mind's own energy, from suggestions by some invisible and unknown spirit, or from another cause still less known to us? We acknowledge that many perceptions do not actually arise from anything external, as in dreams, madness, and other illnesses. Nothing is more inexplicable than how a body could act on a mind so as to convey its image to a substance supposedly so different, even opposite, in nature.

Whether sensory perceptions are produced by external objects resembling them is a question of fact. How can we settle it? Surely through experience, like every similar question. Yet here experience is, and must remain, entirely silent. Only perceptions are ever present to the mind. It cannot possibly experience their connection with objects. The supposition of such a connection therefore has no foundation in reasoning.

120. To appeal to the supreme Being's truthfulness in order to establish the truthfulness of our senses surely takes a very unexpected detour. If his truthfulness were involved in this matter at all, our senses would have to be completely infallible, since he cannot possibly ever deceive. This is to say nothing of the further difficulty: once the external world's existence is questioned, we shall struggle to find arguments proving that Being's existence or any of his attributes.

121. On this subject, therefore, the deeper and more philosophical sceptics will always triumph when they try to introduce universal doubt into every area of human knowledge and inquiry. They may ask: do you trust the senses' truthfulness by following natural instincts and inclinations? These lead you to believe that the perception or sensory image itself is the external object. Do you reject this principle for the more rational opinion that perceptions merely represent something external? Then you abandon your natural inclinations and most obvious feelings. Yet you cannot satisfy reason either, since it can find no convincing experiential argument proving a connection between perceptions and external objects.

122. Another sceptical argument of this kind comes from the deepest philosophy. It might deserve attention if we needed to dive so far to find reasoning that serves so little serious purpose. Modern investigators universally grant that all an object's sensory qualities—hard, soft, hot, cold, white, black, and so on—are merely secondary. They exist not in the objects themselves but as perceptions in the mind, with no external archetype or model that they represent. If this is admitted for secondary qualities, it must also follow for the supposed primary qualities of extension and solidity. The latter have no better claim to that name than the former. We acquire the idea of extension entirely through sight and touch. If all qualities perceived by the senses belong to the mind rather than the object, that conclusion must apply to extension too, since it depends wholly on sensory ideas, or ideas of secondary qualities. We can escape this conclusion only by asserting that ideas of primary qualities are acquired through _Abstraction_. Close examination shows that opinion to be unintelligible and even absurd. We cannot conceive an extension neither touchable nor visible. An extension we can touch or see, yet which is neither hard nor soft, black nor white, is equally beyond human conception. Let anyone try to conceive a triangle in general, neither _Isosceles_ nor _Scalenum_, with no particular length or proportion of sides. He will soon recognize the absurdity of all the scholastic notions about abstraction and general ideas.[31]

[31] This argument comes from Dr. Berkeley. Indeed, most of that exceptionally ingenious author's writings offer the finest lessons in scepticism to be found among ancient or modern philosophers, including Bayle. On his title page, however, he declares—and undoubtedly with complete truth—that he wrote his book against sceptics as well as atheists and free-thinkers. Yet his arguments, despite his different intention, are merely sceptical in reality. This is evident from the fact _that they admit of no answer and produce no conviction_. Their only effect is the momentary bewilderment, uncertainty, and confusion that scepticism produces.

123. The first philosophical objection to sensory evidence, or to belief in external existence, is therefore this: if that belief rests on natural instinct, it contradicts reason; if it appeals to reason, it contradicts natural instinct while offering no rational evidence to convince an impartial inquirer. The second objection goes further and presents the belief as contrary to reason—at least if reason establishes the principle that all sensory qualities belong to the mind rather than the object. Strip matter of every intelligible quality, primary and secondary, and you in a sense annihilate it. You leave only an unknown, inexplicable _something_ as the cause of our perceptions: so imperfect a notion that no sceptic will think it worth disputing.

chapters.title: Section 12: OF THE ACADEMICAL OR SCEPTICAL PHILOSOPHY. — Part 2
paragraphs: 124. Trying to overthrow _reason_ through argument and reasoning may seem an extravagant undertaking for sceptics. Yet this is the great aim of all their inquiries and disputes. They seek objections both to our abstract reasoning and to our reasoning about matters of fact and existence.

The principal objection to all _abstract_ reasoning comes from the ideas of space and time. In everyday life, viewed casually, these ideas are very clear and intelligible. But under the scrutiny of the deeper sciences, whose chief subject they are, they yield principles apparently full of absurdity and contradiction. No priestly _dogmas_ designed to tame and subdue humanity's rebellious reason have ever offended common sense more than the doctrine of extension's infinite divisibility and its consequences, which all geometers and metaphysicians display so pompously, with a kind of triumphant exultation. A real quantity infinitely smaller than any finite quantity, containing quantities infinitely smaller than itself, and so on _in infinitum_: this structure is so bold and prodigious that no claimed demonstration can bear its weight. It contradicts the clearest and most natural principles of human reason.[32] More extraordinary still, these seemingly absurd opinions rest on a chain of the clearest, most natural reasoning. We cannot accept the premises without accepting the consequences. Nothing is more convincing or satisfactory than the conclusions about the properties of circles and triangles. Yet once we accept them, how can we deny that the angle of contact between a circle and its tangent is infinitely smaller than any angle formed by straight lines? How deny that, as we enlarge the circle's diameter _in infinitum_, this angle of contact diminishes still further, even _in infinitum_? Or that angles of contact between other curves and their tangents may be infinitely smaller than those between any circle and its tangent, and so on _in infinitum_? The demonstration of these principles seems as flawless as the proof that a triangle's three angles equal two right angles. Yet the latter conclusion is natural and easy, while the former teem with contradiction and absurdity. Reason seems thrown into bewilderment and suspense, which make her distrust herself and the ground beneath her without any sceptic prompting her. She sees a bright light illuminating certain places, but bordering on the deepest darkness. Between the two she is so dazzled and confused that she can scarcely judge any single object with certainty and assurance.

[32] Whatever disputes arise about mathematical points, we must admit physical points exist: parts of extension that neither the eye nor the imagination can divide or reduce. These images present to imagination or the senses are therefore absolutely indivisible. Mathematicians must consequently admit that they are infinitely smaller than any real part of extension. Yet nothing seems more certain to reason than that an infinite number of them makes an infinite extension. How much more, then, an infinite number of those infinitely small parts of extension that are themselves still supposed infinitely divisible.

125. If possible, the absurdity of these bold conclusions in the abstract sciences becomes still more obvious when we consider time rather than extension. An infinite number of real portions of time passing successively, each exhausted in turn, seems so plainly contradictory that one would think nobody could accept it unless the sciences had corrupted his judgment instead of improving it.

Yet reason must remain restless and uneasy even about the scepticism into which these apparent absurdities and contradictions drive her. How a clear, distinct idea could contain anything contradicting itself or another clear, distinct idea is utterly incomprehensible, and perhaps as absurd as any proposition we could frame. Nothing, therefore, could be more sceptical, more filled with doubt and hesitation, than this very scepticism arising from certain paradoxical conclusions of geometry, or the science of quantity.[33]

[33] I think these absurdities and contradictions might be avoided if we admitted that, strictly speaking, abstract or general ideas do not exist. Every general idea is really a particular idea attached to a general term. As occasion requires, that term recalls other particular ideas resembling the one before the mind in certain respects. Thus, on hearing the word Horse, we immediately picture a black or white animal of a particular size and shape. But the term also commonly applies to animals of other colours, shapes, and sizes. Although their ideas are not actually present to our imagination, we readily recall them, and our reasoning and conclusions proceed as if they were present. If we admit this—as seems reasonable—it follows that all ideas of quantity used by mathematicians are simply particular ideas supplied by the senses and imagination. Consequently, they cannot be infinitely divisible. For now, merely offering this hint is enough; I shall not pursue it further. All lovers of science certainly have an interest in avoiding conclusions that expose them to the ridicule and contempt of the ignorant. This seems the most straightforward solution to these difficulties.

126. Sceptical objections to _moral_ evidence, or reasoning about matters of fact, are either _popular_ or _philosophical_. Popular objections arise from the natural weakness of human understanding; the conflicting opinions held in different ages and nations; changes in our judgment between illness and health, youth and old age, prosperity and adversity; the continual contradictions in each person's opinions and feelings; and many similar considerations. There is no need to dwell further on them. These objections are weak. In ordinary life we reason about fact and existence at every moment, and cannot possibly survive without continually using this kind of argument. Popular objections drawn from such considerations therefore cannot destroy that evidence. Action, employment, and everyday occupations are the great destroyers of _Pyrrhonism_, or excessive scepticism. Its principles may flourish and triumph in the schools, where refuting them is indeed difficult, perhaps impossible. But once they leave that shelter, real objects that stir our passions and feelings confront them with stronger principles of our nature. They vanish like smoke, leaving the most determined sceptic in the same condition as other mortals.

127. The sceptic would therefore do better to stay within his proper field and present the _philosophical_ objections arising from deeper research. Here he seems to have ample grounds for triumph. He rightly insists that all evidence for matters of fact beyond the testimony of sense or memory comes entirely from the relation of cause and effect. We have no idea of this relation beyond two objects frequently _conjoined_. No argument convinces us that objects frequently conjoined in our experience will be conjoined in the same way in other instances. Only custom, or a certain natural instinct, leads to that inference. Though difficult to resist, this instinct may, like other instincts, mislead and deceive. By insisting on these points, the sceptic displays his strength—or rather his own weakness and ours—and seems, at least for the moment, to destroy all assurance and conviction. We could develop these arguments at greater length if any lasting good or benefit to society could ever be expected from them.

128. Here lies the chief and most devastating objection to _excessive_ scepticism: while it retains its full force and vigour, it can never produce lasting good. We need only ask such a sceptic, _What his meaning is? And what he proposes by all these curious researches?_ He immediately finds himself at a loss for an answer. A Copernican or Ptolemaic defending his respective astronomical system may hope to give his audience a stable, lasting conviction. A Stoic or Epicurean presents principles that may not endure but do affect conduct and behaviour. A Pyrrhonian, however, cannot expect his philosophy to influence the mind permanently, or, if it did, to benefit society. On the contrary, if he admits anything, he must admit that human life would perish if his principles prevailed universally and consistently. All speech and action would immediately stop. People would remain completely inactive until their unmet natural needs ended their miserable existence. Admittedly, we need hardly fear so fatal an outcome. Nature is always stronger than principle. A Pyrrhonian's profound reasoning may briefly bewilder and confuse himself or others, but life's first and most trivial event will scatter his doubts and scruples. In every matter of action and speculation, it will leave him exactly like philosophers of every other school, or people who have never bothered with philosophical inquiry. Waking from his dream, he will be the first to join the laughter at himself and admit that his objections are mere amusement. They can do nothing beyond displaying humanity's peculiar condition: we must act, reason, and believe, although our most diligent inquiries cannot satisfy us about the foundations of these operations or remove the objections that may be raised against them.

chapters.title: Section 12: OF THE ACADEMICAL OR SCEPTICAL PHILOSOPHY. — Part 0
paragraphs: 129. There is, however, a more _mitigated_ scepticism, or _academical_ philosophy, that can be both lasting and useful. It may arise partly from Pyrrhonism, or _excessive_ scepticism, when common sense and reflection correct its indiscriminate doubts to some extent. Most people naturally incline towards confident, dogmatic opinions. Seeing only one side of an object, with no conception of a counterbalancing argument, they rush into the principles that attract them and show no tolerance towards opposing views. Hesitation or weighing alternatives confuses their understanding, checks their passions, and interrupts their actions. They are therefore impatient to escape a condition so uncomfortable to them. No force of assertion or stubbornness of belief seems enough to carry them far away from it. But suppose these dogmatic reasoners recognized the strange weaknesses of human understanding even at its most perfect, when its judgments are most careful and precise. Such reflection would naturally inspire greater modesty and restraint, reducing both their self-conceit and their prejudice against opponents. The uneducated may reflect on the disposition of learned people, who usually remain hesitant in their judgments despite all the advantages of study and reflection. If any learned person naturally inclines towards arrogance and obstinacy, a small dose of Pyrrhonism might lower his pride. It would show him how insignificant his few advantages over others are beside the universal perplexity and confusion inherent in human nature. In general, a degree of doubt, caution, and modesty should always accompany a sound reasoner in every kind of examination and decision.

130. Another kind of _mitigated_ scepticism that may benefit humanity, and may naturally result from Pyrrhonian doubts and scruples, limits our inquiries to subjects best suited to human understanding's narrow capacity. Human _imagination_ naturally soars. Delighting in whatever is distant and extraordinary, it ranges unchecked through the furthest reaches of space and time to escape objects made too familiar by custom. Sound _Judgement_ follows the opposite course. Avoiding remote and lofty inquiries, it confines itself to ordinary life and subjects within daily practice and experience, leaving sublime topics to the embellishments of poets and orators, or the arts of priests and politicians. Nothing helps us reach this beneficial resolution more than becoming thoroughly convinced of the force of Pyrrhonian doubt and of our inability to escape it through anything except the strong power of natural instinct. Those inclined towards philosophy will still pursue their inquiries. They recognize that, besides the immediate pleasure of the occupation, philosophical judgments are simply the reflections of everyday life, arranged systematically and corrected. But they will never be tempted to go beyond ordinary life while they remember their faculties' imperfections, narrow range, and inaccurate operations. We cannot satisfactorily explain why, after a thousand experiments, we believe a stone will fall or fire will burn. Can we then ever satisfy ourselves about judgments concerning the origin of worlds and nature's condition throughout eternity, past and future?

Indeed, restricting our inquiries so narrowly is reasonable in every respect. Even the slightest examination of the human mind's natural powers, compared with their objects, is enough to recommend it to us. We shall then discover which subjects properly belong to science and inquiry.

131. It seems to me that quantity and number are the sole objects of abstract science or demonstration. Every attempt to extend this more perfect kind of knowledge beyond those boundaries is mere sophistry and illusion. Because the components of quantity and number are entirely alike, their relations become complex and entangled. Nothing is more interesting or useful than tracing their equality or inequality through different appearances by various intermediate steps. But all other ideas are clearly distinct and different from one another. Our most searching scrutiny can therefore do no more than observe those differences and, through an obvious reflection, declare that one thing is not another. Any difficulty in these judgments arises solely from words with unsettled meanings, which more accurate definitions can correct. However precisely we define the terms, we cannot know _the square of the hypothenuse is equal to the squares of the other two sides_ without a sequence of reasoning and inquiry. But to convince us of the proposition _that where there is no property, there can be no injustice_, we need only define the terms and explain injustice as a violation of property. This proposition is really just a less perfect definition. The same holds for all the supposedly syllogistic reasoning found in every branch of learning except the sciences of quantity and number. These, I think, may safely be called the only proper objects of knowledge and demonstration.

132. Every other human inquiry concerns only matters of fact and existence, which plainly cannot be demonstrated. Whatever _is_ may _not be_. Denying a fact cannot involve a contradiction. Without exception, the idea of any being's non-existence is as clear and distinct as the idea of its existence. However false a proposition denying its existence may be, it is no less conceivable and intelligible than one affirming it. The sciences properly so called are different. In them, every untrue proposition is confused and unintelligible. Saying that the cube root of 64 equals half of 10 is false and can never be distinctly conceived. Saying that Caesar, the angel Gabriel, or any being never existed may also be false, but it remains perfectly conceivable and contains no contradiction.

A being's existence can therefore be proved only through arguments from its cause or its effect, and those arguments rest wholly on experience. If we reason _a priori_, anything may appear capable of producing anything. For all we know, a falling pebble might extinguish the sun, or a person's wish control the planets in their orbits. Experience alone teaches us the nature and limits of cause and effect, allowing us to infer one object's existence from another's[34]. This is the foundation of moral reasoning, which makes up most human knowledge and supplies the source of all human action and behaviour.

[34] Under this philosophy, the impious maxim of ancient philosophy, _Ex nihilo, nihil fit_, which ruled out matter's creation, ceases to be a maxim. Not only might the supreme Being's will create matter: for all we know _a priori_, the will of any other being might create it, as might any other cause the most fanciful imagination could propose.

Moral reasoning concerns either particular facts or general ones. Every practical deliberation in life concerns particular facts, as do all investigations in history, chronology, geography, and astronomy.
The sciences concerned with general facts include politics, natural philosophy, medicine, chemistry, and so on. They investigate the qualities, causes, and effects of an entire species of objects.

Divinity or Theology, when proving a Deity's existence and the immortality of souls, combines reasoning about particular facts with reasoning about general ones. To the extent that experience supports it, it rests on _reason_. Yet its best and firmest foundation is _faith_ and divine revelation.

Morals and criticism belong more properly to taste and feeling than to the understanding. We feel beauty, whether moral or natural, rather than perceive it. If we reason about beauty and try to establish a standard for it, we turn to a new fact: humanity's general tastes, or some similar fact open to reasoning and inquiry.

What havoc must we cause when we search through libraries convinced of these principles? Take any volume in hand—divinity or scholastic metaphysics, for example—and ask: _Does it contain any abstract reasoning concerning quantity or number?_ No. _Does it contain any experimental reasoning concerning matter of fact and existence?_ No. Then throw it into the flames, for it can contain only sophistry and illusion.
